steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on (\sigma,\delta)-polycyclic codes in Ore extensions over finite rings that need not be commutative. Give the background and prior work on these codes, then lay out what we do (duality, isometric equivalence, a Mattson-Solomon transform, decomposition) and close with the structure of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Ore extensions and (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes
2. Boucher and Ulmer's work over finite fields
3. Further literature and terminology
4. Our setting and duality
5. Isometric equivalence, Mattson-Solomon transform, decomposition
6. Structure of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Setting
- R finite ring with unit, \sigma\in\operatorname{End}(R), \delta additive endomorphism with \delta(ab)=\sigma(a)\delta(b)+\delta(a)b
- Ore extension R[x,\sigma,\delta]: xa=\sigma(a)x+\delta(a), x^{r}x^{s}=x^{r+s}
- (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over R: novel topic; ideals (submodules) in S/Sf, S = R[x,\sigma,\delta], Sf two-sided (one-sided) ideal
- generalizes skew cyclic, skew negacyclic, skew constacyclic, polycyclic codes, etc.
- studying them -> unification of approaches, survey of all these generalizations

2. Boucher and Ulmer (2012)
- introduced as submodules in S/Sf, R = \mathbb{F}_{q}
- R=\mathbb{F}_{q}: \sigma -derivations uniquely \delta(a)=\beta(\sigma(a)-a), \beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}
- z=x+\beta: bijective ring homomorphism \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma,\delta] -> \mathbb{F}_{q}[z,\sigma]
- preserves neither Hamming nor rank distance -> new codes, not isometrically equivalent to skew cyclic codes
- improved distance bounds vs skew cyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma]

3. Other work
- limited literature
- generator and parity-check matrices over rings
- over \mathbb{F}_{q}: T_{C_{f}} -invariant linear codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}; T_{C_{f}} = (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation, C_{f} companion matrix of f; special f -> invariant subspaces, generalizing earlier main results
- T_{C_{f}} generalized to T_{M}, M arbitrary matrix -> T_{M} -invariant linear codes
- applications: good quantum codes; \mathbb{Z} -lattices in \mathbb{R}^{N}
- names used: “ (\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (f,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (M,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “skew generalized cyclic codes” = one concept (polycyclic codes generalized to R[x,\sigma,\delta]); we say “ (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes”

4. This paper: setting + duality
- submodules in S/Sf, R finite, not necessarily commutative; first attempt for non-commutative R
- problem: Euclidean duals not (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic
- (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformations -> non-degenerate sesquilinear form \langle\,,\,\rangle_{0}; left/right duals stay (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic

5. Further results
- isometric equivalence: monomial B with C_{f_{1}}B=\sigma(B)C_{f_{2}}+\delta(B) -> codes in S/Sf_{1}, S/Sf_{2} Hamming isometrically equivalent
- Mattson-Solomon transform (minimal generator polynomials, Reed-Solomon codes) -> define in Ore extension setting
- Wedderburn polynomials (Lam and Leroy, R division ring); simple-root if f Wedderburn
- R field: Wedderburn polynomials (x-a_{1})\cdots(x-a_{n}), a_{i} distinct -> generalizes simple-root polycyclic codes
- motivation: invertibility of (\sigma,\delta) -Vandermond matrix (Theorem 5.8)
- decomposition: simple-root C = direct sum of simple-root C_{i}, each C_{i} tied to an eigenvalue of T_{C_{f}}

6. Structure
- Sec 2 Ore extension foundations; Secs 3-4 right/left polycyclic and sequential codes; Sec 5 left/right dualities; Sec 6 Hamming isometry; Sec 7 Mattson-Solomon maps; Sec 8 decomposition

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Let R be a finite ring with unit, \sigma\in\operatorname{End}(R) and \delta an additive endomorphism of R with \delta(ab)=\sigma(a)\delta(b)+\delta(a)b for all a,b\in R. An Ore extension is a non-commutative polynomial ring R[x,\sigma,\delta] where the multiplication is given by xa=\sigma(a)x+\delta(a) and x^{r}x^{s}=x^{r+s}. In coding theory, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over the ring R are a new topic of study. These codes are defined as ideals (submodules) in the quotient ring (quotient module) S/Sf, where S is the Ore extension R[x,\sigma,\delta] and Sf is a two-sided (one-sided) ideal. This class of codes is a powerful generalization, and it includes many generalizations of cyclic codes such as skew cyclic codes, skew negacyclic codes, skew constacyclic codes, polycyclic codes and so on. So if we study (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes from several points of view, we get a unification of the different approaches and a comprehensive survey of all of these generalizations.

Boucher and Ulmer introduced the concept of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in 2012 as submodules in S/Sf, where R is the finite field \mathbb{F}_{q}. It is well-known that when R=\mathbb{F}_{q}, every \sigma -derivation \delta is uniquely determined by \delta(a)=\beta(\sigma(a)-a), where \beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. They proved that with z=x+\beta there is a bijective ring homomorphism between the Ore extension \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma,\delta] and the skew polynomial ring \mathbb{F}_{q}[z,\sigma]. But this homomorphism does not preserve the Hamming distance, and it does not preserve the rank distance either. Because of this, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma,\delta] give new codes which are not isometrically equivalent to skew cyclic codes in the skew polynomial ring \mathbb{F}_{q}[z,\sigma]. They also showed that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes can give better distance bounds than skew cyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma].

Not much has been written on (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. One paper found the generator and parity-check matrices of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over rings. In another paper, it is proven that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over \mathbb{F}_{q} are T_{C_{f}} -invariant linear codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, where T_{C_{f}} is a (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation and C_{f} is the companion matrix associated with f. With a special assumption on f, they looked at (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as invariant subspaces and generalized some of the main results of earlier papers. A later paper went a step further and generalized the (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation T_{C_{f}} to the transformation T_{M}, where M is an arbitrary matrix. Then they generalized the (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over fields to T_{M} -invariant linear codes. As for applications, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes were used to construct good quantum codes, and they were also used to construct \mathbb{Z} -lattices in \mathbb{R}^{N}. It is worth noting that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes are called by different names in these references, like “ (\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (f,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (M,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, and “skew generalized cyclic codes”. All of these terms mean one concept, which is the generalization of polycyclic codes from earlier work into the non-commutative polynomial ring R[x,\sigma,\delta]. In this paper we use the term “ (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes” for this concept.

- our aim: (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as submodules in S/Sf, R finite, not necessarily commutative; first attempt in non-commutative R
- Euclidean duals not (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic -> (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformations give non-degenerate sesquilinear form \langle\,,\,\rangle_{0}; left and right duals stay (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic
- isometric equivalence: monomial B with C_{f_{1}}B=\sigma(B)C_{f_{2}}+\delta(B) -> codes in S/Sf_{1} and S/Sf_{2} Hamming isometrically equivalent
- Mattson-Solomon transform (minimal generator polynomials, Reed-Solomon codes) in Ore extension setting via Wedderburn polynomials (Lam and Leroy, division rings); simple-root if f Wedderburn; over a field (x-a_{1})\cdots(x-a_{n}), a_{i} distinct; motivation: invertible (\sigma,\delta) -Vandermond matrix (Theorem 5.8)
- decomposition: simple-root C = direct sum of simple-root C_{i}, each tied to an eigenvalue of T_{C_{f}}
- structure: Sec 2 Ore extensions; Secs 3-4 right/left polycyclic and sequential codes; Sec 5 dualities; Sec 6 Hamming isometry; Sec 7 Mattson-Solomon maps; Sec 8 decomposition

steps.text:

They also showed that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes can give better distance bounds than skew cyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma].

Not much has been written on (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. One paper found the generator and parity-check matrices of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over rings. In another paper, it is proven that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over \mathbb{F}_{q} are T_{C_{f}} -invariant linear codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, where T_{C_{f}} is a (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation and C_{f} is the companion matrix associated with f. With a special assumption on f, they looked at (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as invariant subspaces and generalized some of the main results of earlier papers. A later paper went a step further and generalized the (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation T_{C_{f}} to the transformation T_{M}, where M is an arbitrary matrix. Then they generalized the (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over fields to T_{M} -invariant linear codes. As for applications, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes were used to construct good quantum codes, and they were also used to construct \mathbb{Z} -lattices in \mathbb{R}^{N}. It is worth noting that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes are called by different names in these references, like “ (\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (f,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (M,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, and “skew generalized cyclic codes”. All of these terms mean one concept, which is the generalization of polycyclic codes from earlier work into the non-commutative polynomial ring R[x,\sigma,\delta]. In this paper we use the term “ (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes” for this concept.

Motivated by these works, in this paper we investigate (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as submodules in S/Sf, where R is a finite ring that is not necessarily commutative. This is the first attempt to study this class of codes in the non-commutative ring R. One challenge with (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes is that their Euclidean duals do not have the structure of a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code. To deal with this, we use (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformations to introduce the non-degenerate sesquilinear form \langle\,,\,\rangle_{0}. We then show that the left and right duals with respect to this form keep their (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code nature.

A well-known problem in coding theory is classifying codes that are isometrically equivalent. We show that if there is a monomial matrix B such that C_{f_{1}}B=\sigma(B)C_{f_{2}}+\delta(B), then (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in S/Sf_{1} and (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in S/Sf_{2} are Hamming isometrically equivalent.

The Mattson-Solomon transform is a well-known mathematical technique with many applications, for example determining minimal generator polynomials and Reed-Solomon codes. Our next challenge is to define the Mattson-Solomon transform in the Ore extension setting. For this we use the theory of Wedderburn polynomials, which Lam and Leroy explored extensively for the case where R is a division ring. We call a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code simple-root if f is a Wedderburn polynomial. Note that when R is a field, the Wedderburn polynomials have the form (x-a_{1})\cdots(x-a_{n}), where the a_{i} s are distinct elements. So the simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes generalize the simple-root polycyclic codes defined in earlier work. The reason we define the (\sigma,\delta) -Mattson-Solomon transform for these specific codes is that the (\sigma,\delta) -Vandermond matrix is invertible, see Theorem 5.8 in their later paper.

The next challenge is decomposing (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. Using the Wedderburn polynomial we define the simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code C, and we decompose it into the direct sum of simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes C_{i}, where each C_{i} is related to an eigenvalue of T_{C_{f}}.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the foundation of Ore extension rings that we need in the later sections. Sections 3 and 4 present the concept of right and left (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic and sequential codes and how they are related. Section 5 gives an alternate concept of left and right dualities, so that the dual of any (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code is still a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code. Section 6 explores the Hamming isometry equivalence of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. Section 7 presents the (\sigma,\delta) -Mattson-Solomon maps for simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. Finally, Section 8 gives a decomposition of a simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Suppose that R is a finite ring with unit, \sigma\in\operatorname{End}(R) and \delta is an additive endomorphism of R satisfying \delta(ab)=\sigma(a)\delta(b)+\delta(a)b for all a,b\in R. An Ore extension is a non-commutative polynomial ring R[x,\sigma,\delta] constructed by the multiplications xa=\sigma(a)x+\delta(a) and x^{r}x^{s}=x^{r+s}. In coding theory, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over the ring R are a novel object of study. These codes are defined as ideals (submodules) in the quotient ring (quotient module) S/Sf, where S is the Ore extension R[x,\sigma,\delta] and Sf is a two-sided (one-sided) ideal. This class of codes is a powerful generalization that encompasses various generalizations of cyclic codes, including skew cyclic codes, skew negacyclic codes, skew constacyclic codes, polycyclic codes, etc, see [1,2,3,4,5,6]. Therefore, by studying (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes from several points of view, we achieve a unification of different approaches and a comprehensive survey of all these generalizations.

In 2012, Boucher and Ulmer introduced the concept of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as submodules in S/Sf, where R is the finite field \mathbb{F}_{q}, see [7]. It is well-known that if R=\mathbb{F}_{q}, then all \sigma -derivations \delta are uniquely determined by \delta(a)=\beta(\sigma(a)-a), where \beta\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. They proved that if z=x+\beta, then there exists a bijective ring homomorphism between the Ore extension \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma,\delta] and the skew polynomial ring \mathbb{F}_{q}[z,\sigma]. However, this homomorphism preserves neither the Hamming distance nor the rank distance. As a result, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma,\delta] produce new codes that are not isometrically equivalent to skew cyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[z,\sigma]. They also demonstrated that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes can provide better distance bounds than skew cyclic codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}[x,\sigma].

There is only a limited account of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. In [8], the authors determined the generator and parity-check matrices of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over rings. In [9], it is proven that (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over \mathbb{F}_{q} are T_{C_{f}} -invariant linear codes in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, where T_{C_{f}} is a (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation and C_{f} is the companion matrix associated with f. Under a special assumption on f, they considered (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as invariant subspaces and generalized some of the main results in [2,10]. In [11], the authors went a step further and generalized the (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformation T_{C_{f}} into the transformation T_{M}, with M an arbitrary matrix, and then generalized (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes over fields into T_{M} -invariant linear codes. As applications, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes were used to establish good quantum codes in [12,13], and to construct \mathbb{Z} -lattices in \mathbb{R}^{N} in [14]. Notably, (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes have been described with different terminologies in these references, such as “ (\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (f,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, “ (M,\sigma,\delta) -codes”, and “skew generalized cyclic codes”. All these terms represent one concept: the generalization of polycyclic codes (see [2]) into the non-commutative polynomial ring R[x,\sigma,\delta]. In this paper, we use the term “ (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes” for this concept.

Motivated by these works, this paper investigates (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes as submodules in S/Sf, where R is a finite, but not necessarily commutative, ring. This is the first attempt to study this class of codes in the non-commutative ring R. A challenging aspect of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes is that their Euclidean duals do not have a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code structure. To address this, we employ (\sigma,\delta) -Pseudo Linear Transformations to introduce the non-degenerate sesquilinear form \langle\,,\,\rangle_{0}, and establish that the left and right duals related to this form preserve their (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code nature.

A well-known problem in coding theory is the classification of isometrically equivalent codes. We establish that if there exists a monomial matrix B such that C_{f_{1}}B=\sigma(B)C_{f_{2}}+\delta(B), then (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in S/Sf_{1} and (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes in S/Sf_{2} are Hamming isometrically equivalent.

The Mattson-Solomon transform is a well-known mathematical technique with diverse applications, including the determination of minimal generator polynomials and Reed-Solomon codes, see [2,15,16]. Our next challenge is to define the Mattson-Solomon transform in the Ore extension setting. To do this, we employ the theory of Wedderburn polynomials, explored extensively by Lam and Leroy in [17,18] when R is a division ring. We classify a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code as simple-root if f is a Wedderburn polynomial. Note that when R is a field, the Wedderburn polynomials have the form (x-a_{1})\cdots(x-a_{n}), where the a_{i} s are distinct elements, see [17]. Therefore, simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes generalize simple-root polycyclic codes as defined in [2]. Our motivation for defining the (\sigma,\delta) -Mattson-Solomon transform for these specific codes is the invertibility of the (\sigma,\delta) -Vandermond matrix, see [18] Theorem 5.8.

The next challenge is the decomposition of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes. Using the Wedderburn polynomial, we define the simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code C and decompose it into the direct sum of simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes C_{i}, such that each C_{i} is related to an eigenvalue of T_{C_{f}}.

The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, the foundation of Ore extension rings for the subsequent sections is introduced. In Sections 3 and 4, the concept of right and left (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic and sequential codes and their relationships are presented. In Section 5, an alternate concept of left and right dualities is offered, which ensures that the dual of any (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code remains a (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code. In Section 6, the Hamming isometry equivalence of (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes is explored. In Section 7, the (\sigma,\delta) -Mattson-Solomon maps for simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic codes are presented. Finally, in Section 8, a decomposition of a simple-root (\sigma,\delta) -polycyclic code is provided.
